# openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/openssh/latest/target-redirect/openssh/

## Expand description

Scriptable SSH through OpenSSH (**only works on unix**).

This crate wraps the OpenSSH remote login client (`ssh` on most machines), and provides
a convenient mechanism for running commands on remote hosts. Since all commands are executed
through the `ssh` command, all your existing configuration (e.g., in `.ssh/config`) should
continue to work as expected.

[§](https://docs.rs#executing-remote-processes)Executing remote processes

The library’s API is modeled closely after that of [ std::process::Command](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html), since

`ssh` also
attempts to make the remote process seem as much as possible like a local command. However,
there are some differences.First of all, all remote commands are executed in the context of a single ssh
[session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html). Authentication happens once when the session is
[established](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.connect), and subsequent command invocations re-use the same connection.

Note that the maximum number of multiplexed remote commands is 10 by default. This value can be
increased by changing the `MaxSessions` setting in [ sshd_config](https://linux.die.net/man/5/sshd_config).

Much like with [ std::process::Command](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html), you have multiple
options when it comes to launching a remote command. You can

[spawn](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.spawn)the remote command, which just gives you a handle to the running process, you can run the command and wait for its

[output](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.output), or you can run it and just extract its

[exit status](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.status). Unlike its

`std`
counterpart though, these methods on [can fail even if the remote command executed successfully, since there is a fallible network separating you from it.](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html)

`OwningCommand`Also unlike its `std` counterpart, [ spawn](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.spawn) gives you a

[rather than a](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html)

`Child`[. Behind the scenes, a remote child is really just a process handle to the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Child.html)

`std::process::Child`*local*

`ssh` instance corresponding to the spawned remote command. The behavior
of the methods of [therefore match the behavior of](https://docs.rs/type.RemoteChild.html)

`RemoteChild``ssh`, rather than that of
the remote command directly. Usually, these are the same, though not always, as highlighted in
the documetantation the individual methods. See also the section below on Remote Shells.[§](https://docs.rs#connection-modes)Connection modes

This library provides two way to connect to the [ ControlMaster](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/OpenSSH/Cookbook/Multiplexing):

One is to spawn a new process, the other is to connect to the control socket directly.

The process implementation executes remote commands by invoking the ssh command locally with arguments that make the invocation reuse the connections set up by the control master.

This maximizes compatibility with OpenSSH, but loses out on some fidelity in information about execution since only the exit code and the output of the ssh command is available to inspect.

The native mux implementation on the other hand connects directly to the ssh control master and executes commands and retrieves the exit codes and the output of the remote process over its native protocol.

This gives better access to error information at the cost of introducing more non-OpenSSH code into the call path.

The former parses the stdout/stderr of the ssh control master to retrieve the error for any failed operations, while the later retrieves the error from the control socket directly.

Thus, the error handling in the later is more robust.

Also, the former requires one process to be spawn for every connection while the later only needs to create one socket, so the later has better performance and consumes less resource.

Behind the scenes, the crate uses ssh’s [ ControlMaster](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/OpenSSH/Cookbook/Multiplexing) feature to multiplex the channels for
the different remote commands. Because of this, each remote command is tied to the lifetime of
the

[that spawned them. When the session is](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html)

`Session`[closed](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.close), the connection is severed, and there can be no outstanding remote clients.

[§](https://docs.rs#authentication)Authentication

This library supports only password-less authentication schemes. If running `ssh` to a target
host requires you to provide input on standard input (`STDIN`), then this crate will not work
for you. You should set up keypair-based authentication instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Since we are wrapping the `ssh`, which in turn runs a remote command that we do not control, we
do not have a reliable way to tell the difference between what is a failure of the SSH
connection itself, and what is a program error from the remote host. We do our best with some
heuristics (like `ssh` exiting with status code 255 if a connection error occurs), but the
errors from this crate will almost necessarily be worse than those of a native SSH
implementation. Sorry in advance :)

This also means that you may see strange errors when the remote process is terminated by a
signal (such as through `kill` or `pkill`). When this happens, all the local ssh program sees
is that the remote process disappeared, and so it returns with an error. It does not
communicate that the process exited due to a signal. In cases like this, your call will return
[ Error::Disconnected](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.Disconnected), because the connection to

*that*remote process was disconnected. The ssh connection as a whole is likely still intact.

To check if the connection has truly failed, use [ Session::check](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.check). It will return

`Ok` if the
master connection is still operational, and *may*provide you with more information than you got from the failing command (that is, just

[) if it is not.](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.Disconnected)

`Error::Disconnected`[§](https://docs.rs#remote-shells)Remote Shells

When you invoke a remote command through ssh, the remote command is executed by a shell on the
remote end. That shell *interprets* anything passed to it — it might evalute words starting
with `$` as variables, split arguments by whitespace, and other things a shell is wont to do.
Since that is *usually* not what you expect to happen, `.arg("a b")` should pass a *single*
argument with the value `a b`, `openssh` *escapes* every argument (and the command itself) by
default using [ shell-escape](https://crates.io/crates/shell-escape). This works well in most cases, but might run into issues when
the remote shell (generally the remote user’s login shell) has a different syntax than the
shell

`shell-escape` targets (bash). For example, Windows shells have different escaping syntax
than bash does.If this applies to you, you can use [ raw_arg](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.raw_arg),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.raw_args)

`raw_args`[to bypass the escaping that](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.raw_command)

`raw_command``openssh` normally does for you.[§](https://docs.rs#sftp-subsystem)Sftp subsystem

For sftp and other ssh subsystem, check [ Session::subsystem](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.subsystem) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use openssh::{Session, KnownHosts};
let session = Session::connect_mux("me@ssh.example.com", KnownHosts::Strict).await?;
let ls = session.command("ls").output().await?;
eprintln!("{}", String::from_utf8(ls.stdout).expect("server output was not valid UTF-8"));
let whoami = session.command("whoami").output().await?;
assert_eq!(whoami.stdout, b"me\n");
session.close().await?;
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# mediaschema - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mediaschema/0.2.1/mediaschema/

## Expand description

Product-agnostic media-primitive schema.

The architectural hub is the hand-written [ domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html) layer; every
backend — protobuf wire (under [

`buffa`]), `sqlx` row mappers
(under [`sqlx`]), MongoDB (under [`mongodb`]) — is a thin lossless
conversion to/from the domain. Locked schema docs live under
`schema/*.md`; they are the specification the implementation tracks.Encode-side bridges (`From<&Domain> for Backend`) are infallible —
the domain is the validated side. Decode-side bridges
(`TryFrom<Backend> for Domain`) route through the same `try_new` +
`with_*` builders application code uses, so every invariant is
re-enforced at the wire/storage edge.

[§](https://docs.rs#aggregate-clusters)Aggregate clusters

- `domain::Media`- `domain::MediaFile`- `domain::WatchedLocation`
- `domain::Audio`- `domain::AudioTrack`- `domain::AudioSegment`- `Word`child) — audio cluster.
- `domain::Video`- `domain::VideoTrack`- `domain::Scene`- `domain::Keyframe`
- `domain::Subtitle`- `domain::SubtitleTrack`- `domain::SubtitleCue`- `<Id, D>`— subtitle cluster; cues are polymorphic over the per-format payload- `D`(- `SrtData`,- `VttData`,- `AssData`,- `LrcData`).
- `domain::Person`- `domain::Speaker`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

Three independent **capability tiers** (`alloc` / `std`, both
additive), three **medium-aggregate gates** (`video` / `audio` /
`subtitle`), plus optional **backend** features. Defaults are
`std + video + audio + subtitle`.

| flag | role | depends on |
|---|---|---|
| none | no-std + no-alloc; stack-only types only | — |
| `alloc` | no-std + alloc; adds heap-using domain types | — |
| `std`(default) | adds `jiff`-using aggregates +`Uuid::now_v7` | — |
| `video`(default) | compiles the `Video`/`VideoTrack`/`Scene`/`Keyframe`aggregate tree + its backends | a heap tier |
| `audio`(default) | compiles the `Audio`/`AudioTrack`/`AudioSegment`aggregate tree + its backends | a heap tier |
| `subtitle`(default) | compiles the `Subtitle`/`SubtitleTrack`/`SubtitleCue`aggregate tree + its backends | a heap tier |
| `buffa` | proto3 wire layer (under [ `buffa`]) | `std`or`alloc` |
| `json` | wire JSON via serde | `std + buffa` |
| `arbitrary` | `Arbitrary`derives for property tests | `std + buffa` |
| `mongodb` | bson backend (under [ `mongodb`]) | `std + json` |
| `sqlx-postgres`/`sqlx-mysql`/`sqlx-sqlite` | sql backends (under [ `sqlx`]) | `std` |

The three medium gates are independent on/off flags: a consumer that
only needs the video aggregate tree can opt out of the audio /
subtitle trees (and all their backend bridges) with
`default-features = false` + `features = ["std", "video"]`. The
cross-cutting aggregates (`Media`, `MediaFile`, `Person`, `Speaker`,
`WatchedLocation`, `UserTag`, `SceneAnnotation`) plus the
[ Identified<Id, D>](https://docs.rs/domain/identified/struct.Identified.html) transport envelope are
always available when a heap tier is on.

[§](https://docs.rs#regenerating-wire-code)Regenerating wire code

The buffa-generated wire layer (`src/generated/`) is produced from
the `.proto` files in `proto/`. Regenerate with
`cargo run -p xtask -- gen`. Do **not** hand-edit the generated
files.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::domain::`- [Identified](https://docs.rs/domain/identified/struct.Identified.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html)
- Hand-written domain layer — the architectural hub. App logic programs
against `mediaschema::domain::*`; the buffa-generated wire types at the crate root (re-exported from`generated::media::v1::*`, available with`feature = "std"`) are the serialization edge. Domain ⇄ wire conversions are added incrementally as each aggregate lands (with`domain → wire → domain`round-trip property tests). See`schema/*.md`for the locked specifications. Hand-written domain layer — the architectural hub for mediaschema.
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)- `audio`and- `std`and- `subtitle`and- `video`
- Standalone object-graph types — the “whole record” programming shape.
One graph type per media-tree aggregate, each owning its full field
set: parent FKs and id-vecs are replaced by the nested children
themselves; lifting from the flat aggregates validates parent-child
id coherence. Requires `std`plus all three medium features: a graph is a complete record, so partial-medium consumers use the flat aggregates instead. Standalone object-graph types — the “whole record” programming shape.

# base64_ng_sanitization - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng-sanitization/1.3.0/base64_ng_sanitization/

## Expand description

Optional `sanitization` integration helpers for `base64-ng`.

This crate deliberately lives outside the core `base64-ng` package so the
base crate keeps its zero-runtime-dependency contract. Applications that
already admit `sanitization` can opt into this companion crate and decode
secret-bearing Base64 directly into `sanitization` secret containers.

The extension trait targets [ base64_ng::ct::CtEngine](https://docs.rs/base64-ng/1.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/base64_ng/ct/struct.CtEngine.html) rather than the
ordinary strict decoder.

`sanitization` 1.2.2’s native [primitives are re-exported for callers that want](https://docs.rs/ct/index.html)

`ct``Choice`-based verification after decode.
Enable `memory-lock` or `high-assurance` for locked secret containers on
supported native targets.```
use base64_ng::ct;
use base64_ng_sanitization::{CtDecodeSanitizationExt, SanitizationCtEqExt};
let secret = ct::STANDARD
    .decode_secret_bytes::<5>(b"aGVsbG8=")
    .unwrap();
assert!(secret.sanitization_verify(b"hello", "example declassifies equality"));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ct](https://docs.rs/ct/index.html)
- Data-oblivious primitives for secret-handling code.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Sanitization](https://docs.rs/enum.SanitizationDecodeError.html)- Decode - Error
- Error returned by fixed-size sanitization decode helpers.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [CtDecode](https://docs.rs/trait.CtDecodeSanitizationExt.html)- Sanitization - Ext
- Extension helpers for decoding with `base64_ng::ct::CtEngine``sanitization`secret containers.
- [Sanitization](https://docs.rs/trait.SanitizationCtEqExt.html)- CtEq - Ext
- Native `sanitization::ct`comparison helpers for decoded secret containers.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sanitization_](https://docs.rs/fn.sanitization_ct_eq_public_len.html)- ct_ - eq_ - public_ - len
- Compare two byte slices through `sanitization::ct`with public length.

# bamboo_sdk - Rust

## Expand description

Ergonomic top-level Agent SDK facade for the Bamboo agent framework.

This crate is the thin, ergonomic entry point over the engine runtime. It
depends only on the lower layers (`bamboo-engine`, `bamboo-infrastructure`,

See [ agent](https://docs.rs/agent/index.html) for the full surface; the most common entry points are

# bamboo_notification - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-notification/2026.7.3/bamboo_notification/

## Expand description

Notification policy for the Bamboo agent framework.

This crate owns the *decision* of whether a given [ AgentEvent](https://docs.rs/bamboo-agent-core/2026.7.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bamboo_agent_core/agent/events/enum.AgentEvent.html) should
surface to the user as a notification. It is deliberately a self-contained
infra crate with no I/O beyond reading/writing a small preferences file and
no async runtime: it classifies events, gates them against user

[, and coalesces duplicates within a short window.](https://docs.rs/preferences/struct.NotificationPreferences.html)

`NotificationPreferences`The pipeline is three layers:

- `preferences`
- `policy`- `classify`- `AgentEvent`- `ClassifiedNotification`
- `service`- `Send + Sync`- `NotificationService`- `Arc`.

The server constructs the user-facing
[ AgentEvent::Notification](https://docs.rs/bamboo-agent-core/2026.7.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bamboo_agent_core/agent/events/enum.AgentEvent.html#variant.Notification);
the client merely delivers it after its own presence checks.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use policy::`- [NotificationCategory](https://docs.rs/policy/enum.NotificationCategory.html);
- `pub use policy::`- [NotificationPriority](https://docs.rs/policy/enum.NotificationPriority.html);
- `pub use preferences::`- [NotificationPreferences](https://docs.rs/preferences/struct.NotificationPreferences.html);
- `pub use service::`- [NotificationService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.NotificationService.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [policy](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html)
- Pure classification of agent events into candidate notifications.
- [preferences](https://docs.rs/preferences/index.html)
- User preferences gating which agent events become notifications.
- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- Stateful notification service wrapping the pure `crate::policy`

# bamboo_permission - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-permission/2026.7.3/bamboo_permission/

## Expand description

Permission management system for tool execution.

This module provides a comprehensive permission system for controlling access to potentially dangerous operations like file writes, command execution, HTTP requests, and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-components)Key Components

- `PermissionConfig`
- `PermissionChecker`
- `PermissionType`

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use crate::{PermissionConfig, PermissionChecker, PermissionType};
// Create a permission configuration
let config = Arc::new(PermissionConfig::new());
// Check if permission is needed
if config.needs_confirmation(PermissionType::WriteFile, "/tmp/test.txt") {
    // Request user confirmation...
}
// Grant session permission
config.grant_session_permission(PermissionType::WriteFile, "/tmp/*");
```

# llm-ping 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/llm-ping/0.1.0

# llm-ping

Detailed latency diagnostic for LLM API endpoints. Measures each phase of a request (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP first byte, time-to-first-token (TTFT), generation throughput, and end-to-end total) decomposed per request.

## Install

```
# or from source:
```
## Quick Start

Test a local Ollama instance:

```
```
Test a remote provider with multiple requests:

```
```
## Timing Phases

Each request is broken into the following phases, reported as columns in the results table:

| Phase | Description |
|---|---|
| DNS | DNS resolution — how long to resolve the hostname |
| TCP | TCP connection establishment latency |
| TLS | TLS handshake duration (omitted for plain HTTP) |
| HTTP FB | HTTP first byte — time from sending the request to receiving the first response byte |
| TTFT | Time to first token — latency from request send to first content token in the stream |
| Gen | Generation time — duration from first token to stream completion |
| tok/s | Token throughput during the generation phase only |
| Total | Wall-clock end-to-end time for the entire request |

When `-c N` with `N > 1`, an **Avg** row is appended with per-phase averages and aggregate token throughput.

## CLI Reference

```
Usage: llm-ping [OPTIONS]
Options:
  -p, --provider <PROVIDER>  Provider type [default: ollama]
  -u, --url <URL>            API endpoint URL (default from --provider)
  -m, --model <MODEL>        Model name (default from --provider)
      --prompt <PROMPT>      Prompt text [default: "Introduce yourself in one short sentence."]
  -c, --count <COUNT>        Number of requests [default: 1]
      --warm <WARM>          Warmup requests (not counted in stats) [default: 0]
  -k, --api-key <API_KEY>    API key (default: provider-specific env var)
      --params <PARAMS>      Extra JSON parameters merged into request body
      --no-stream            Non-streaming mode
      --json                 JSON output
      --dry-run              Dry run: print request details without sending
      --quiet                Suppress progress dots
  -v, --verbose...           Verbose output (-v: info, -vv: debug, -vvv: trace)
      --timeout <TIMEOUT>    Request timeout in seconds [default: 60]
  -h, --help                 Print help (see more with '--help')
  -V, --version              Print version
```
## Notes

- **Streaming mode is default.**The- `--no-stream`flag disables streaming — you get generation time but no TTFT.
- **Warmup**(- `--warm N`) sends requests that are discarded from stats. Useful to avoid cold-start artifacts.
- **Progress dots**appear when- `-c`> 1 and are suppressed with- `--quiet`.

# facett_geomap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-geomap/0.1.10/facett_geomap/

## Expand description

**facett-geomap** — a *scrollable & zoomable* geo map. Unlike
[ facett_map::MapView](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.MapView.html) (a static fit-to-rect scatter), this carries a live

**viewport**(centre + zoom) you can pan with the mouse and zoom with the scroll wheel /

`+`/`−`, and it draws **two layers**:

- a **point layer**—`(lon, lat)`population points (small dots), and
- a **cluster-hotspot layer**—`(lon, lat, count, label)`density hotspots drawn as circles**sized by count**with a count badge + label.

Web Mercator (same projection as `facett-map` / osm-viewer), so an optional
**vector basemap** layer (3. below) lines up exactly with the points + hotspots:

- a **basemap layer**— reused`facett_map::Way`*under*the points and hotspots, so the geomap shows a map and not just dots on a flat fill.

The component is a proper [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html): it exposes its full viewport + all three
layers’ summaries as

`state_json` and advertises `scalable` (zoom) so it is
robot-testable and drives through `facett_core::harness` with no display.Source-agnostic: the host loads the points (korp: from the simulated
population’s lat/lon), the hotspots (korp: from the ekonomiskt_bistand cluster
pass), and an optional basemap (korp: real `ways.parquet` via the osm adapter,
or the synthetic znippy-rabbit fallback) and hands them here. **Graceful:** no
ways → the original point + hotspot behaviour, unchanged.

# base64_ng - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng/1.3.0/base64_ng/

## Expand description

`base64-ng` is a `no_std`-first Base64 encoder and decoder.

The core API provides strict RFC 4648-style behavior, caller-owned output
buffers, and an audited scalar fallback. The `1.2.x` line admits selected
SIMD encode acceleration while keeping decode on the scalar foundation.
Any accelerated backend must match the scalar module byte-for-byte and pass
the documented admission evidence before dispatch can select it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Encode and decode with caller-owned buffers:

```
use base64_ng::{STANDARD, checked_encoded_len};
let input = b"hello";
const ENCODED_CAPACITY: usize = match checked_encoded_len(5, true) {
    Some(len) => len,
    None => panic!("encoded length overflow"),
};
let mut encoded = [0u8; ENCODED_CAPACITY];
let encoded_len = STANDARD.encode_slice(input, &mut encoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&encoded[..encoded_len], b"aGVsbG8=");
let mut decoded = [0u8; 5];
let decoded_len = STANDARD.decode_slice(&encoded, &mut decoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&decoded[..decoded_len], input);
```
Use the URL-safe no-padding engine:

```
use base64_ng::URL_SAFE_NO_PAD;
let mut encoded = [0u8; 3];
let encoded_len = URL_SAFE_NO_PAD.encode_slice(b"\xfb\xff", &mut encoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&encoded[..encoded_len], b"-_8");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sensitive-decode-policy)Sensitive Decode Policy

The default engines such as [ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/constant.STANDARD.html) and

[are strict scalar encoders/decoders with localized diagnostics. They are not constant-time token validators or key-material decoders: strict decode and validation may branch or return early based on malformed input, and strict](https://docs.rs/constant.URL_SAFE_NO_PAD.html)

`URL_SAFE_NO_PAD`[values can include input-derived bytes and indexes. Do not log strict decode errors verbatim for secret-bearing input; log](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)

`DecodeError`[instead. Use](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html#method.kind)

`DecodeError::kind`[,](https://docs.rs/ct/constant.STANDARD.html)

`ct::STANDARD`[, or](https://docs.rs/ct/constant.URL_SAFE_NO_PAD.html)

`crate::ct::URL_SAFE_NO_PAD`[for secret-bearing payloads where decode timing posture matters more than exact error indexes.](https://docs.rs/struct.Engine.html#method.ct_decoder)

`Engine::ct_decoder`Recommended heap-owning pattern for secret-bearing standard Base64:

```
use base64_ng::ct;
let expected = b"session-key";
let decoded = ct::STANDARD.decode_secret(b"c2Vzc2lvbi1rZXk=").unwrap();
assert!(decoded.constant_time_eq_public_len(expected));
```
For shared-memory, enclave-adjacent, HSM-style, or multi-principal
deployments where even transient writes into caller-owned output are
unacceptable, use [ ct::CtEngine::decode_slice_staged_clear_tail](https://docs.rs/ct/struct.CtEngine.html#method.decode_slice_staged_clear_tail) with a
private staging buffer.
CT behavior is best-effort and build-profile specific. Link-Time
Optimization can change generated code shape across crate boundaries, so
high-assurance deployments must rerun the dudect and generated-assembly
evidence scripts for their exact compiler, target, feature set, and release
profile before treating CT decode as acceptable.

[§](https://docs.rs#zeroization-caveat)Zeroization Caveat

Cleanup APIs and redacted buffers use dependency-free best-effort wiping:
byte-wise volatile zero writes followed by an architecture-gated inline
assembly barrier plus a hardware store-ordering fence where stable Rust
supports it, and a compiler fence on all targets. This resists common
compiler dead-store elimination and orders the issued zero stores on native
supported architectures, but it is not a formal zeroization guarantee and
cannot clear historical copies, registers, cache lines, write buffers, swap,
hibernation images, core dumps, cold-boot remanence, or OS-level memory
snapshots.
High-assurance applications should apply their own approved zeroization
policy to caller-owned buffers at the protocol boundary. Architectures
without a native wipe barrier fail closed by default unless
`allow-compiler-fence-only-wipe` is enabled after platform review. On
`wasm32`, the wipe barrier is compiler-fence-only and cannot constrain
downstream wasm runtime JITs. For that reason, `wasm32` builds fail closed
by default. Enable `allow-wasm32-best-effort-wipe` only when the deployment
explicitly accepts compiler-fence-only cleanup and applies its own memory
strategy.

# facett_card - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-card/0.1.10/facett_card/

## Expand description

**facett-card** — a YouTrack / Jira-style **record card**: a titled record
with a **typed field grid** ([ CardField](https://docs.rs/struct.CardField.html)) and

**nestable sub-cards**(

[, each in a collapsible header, recursively — a parent issue expands into its sub-tasks). A](https://docs.rs/struct.Card.html#structfield.children)

`Card::children`[is the](https://docs.rs/struct.CardView.html)

`CardView`[driver: it renders the card read-only (theme-aware chips / bars / hyperlinks per field kind), toggles into an](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`**edit form**that

*reuses*

[rather than re-implementing inputs, and serializes the whole card (incl. children) as pretty JSON for](https://docs.rs/facett-form/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_form/index.html)

`facett_form``copy()`.[§](https://docs.rs#why-edit-mode-reuses-facett-form)Why edit-mode reuses facett-form

A card in edit mode is just a *bound form* over the card’s own fields. We make
the card itself the [ FormModel](https://docs.rs/facett-form/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_form/trait.FormModel.html):

[lays each](https://docs.rs/struct.Card.html#method.fields)

`Card::fields`[into the](https://docs.rs/struct.CardField.html)

`CardField`[field-builder with the right widget for its](https://docs.rs/facett-form/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_form/struct.FormUi.html)

`FormUi`[(text / number / select / date / …), and](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldKind.html)

`FieldKind`[/](https://docs.rs/struct.Card.html#method.from_clip)

`Card::from_clip`[round-trip the card as JSON. The hard parts (labels, per-field outlines, the Save/Reset bar, dirty-tracking, clipboard) are facett-form’s — we don’t re-solve them. Sub-cards stay read-mode; expanding one and toggling](https://docs.rs/struct.Card.html#method.to_clip)

`Card::to_clip`*its*edit is the same recursion.

# openssh 0.11.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/openssh/0.11.6

Scriptable SSH through OpenSSH.

This crate wraps the OpenSSH remote login client (`ssh` on most machines), and provides
a convenient mechanism for running commands on remote hosts. Since all commands are executed
through the `ssh` command, all your existing configuration (e.g., in `.ssh/config`) should
continue to work as expected.

The library's API is modeled closely after that of [`std::process::Command`], since `ssh` also
attempts to make the remote process seem as much as possible like a local command.

### Run integration tests

Requires `docker` and [ cargo-hack](https://github.com/taiki-e/cargo-hack).

Check [getting Docker guide](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) on how to install docker,
and use `cargo install cargo-hack` to install [ cargo-hack](https://github.com/taiki-e/cargo-hack).

```
./run_ci_tests.sh
```
It will create a container which runs sshd, setup ssh-agent, and environment variables that are required to run the integration tests.

It will also test different combination of feature flags to ensure they all compile without error.

./build_doc.sh
```

# openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/openssh/0.11.6/target-redirect/openssh/

## Expand description

Scriptable SSH through OpenSSH (**only works on unix**).

This crate wraps the OpenSSH remote login client (`ssh` on most machines), and provides
a convenient mechanism for running commands on remote hosts. Since all commands are executed
through the `ssh` command, all your existing configuration (e.g., in `.ssh/config`) should
continue to work as expected.

[§](https://docs.rs#executing-remote-processes)Executing remote processes

The library’s API is modeled closely after that of [ std::process::Command](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html), since

`ssh` also
attempts to make the remote process seem as much as possible like a local command. However,
there are some differences.First of all, all remote commands are executed in the context of a single ssh
[session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html). Authentication happens once when the session is
[established](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.connect), and subsequent command invocations re-use the same connection.

Note that the maximum number of multiplexed remote commands is 10 by default. This value can be
increased by changing the `MaxSessions` setting in [ sshd_config](https://linux.die.net/man/5/sshd_config).

Much like with [ std::process::Command](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html), you have multiple
options when it comes to launching a remote command. You can

[spawn](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.spawn)the remote command, which just gives you a handle to the running process, you can run the command and wait for its

[output](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.output), or you can run it and just extract its

[exit status](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.status). Unlike its

`std`
counterpart though, these methods on [can fail even if the remote command executed successfully, since there is a fallible network separating you from it.](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html)

`OwningCommand`Also unlike its `std` counterpart, [ spawn](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.spawn) gives you a

[rather than a](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html)

`Child`[. Behind the scenes, a remote child is really just a process handle to the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Child.html)

`std::process::Child`*local*

`ssh` instance corresponding to the spawned remote command. The behavior
of the methods of [therefore match the behavior of](https://docs.rs/type.RemoteChild.html)

`RemoteChild``ssh`, rather than that of
the remote command directly. Usually, these are the same, though not always, as highlighted in
the documetantation the individual methods. See also the section below on Remote Shells.[§](https://docs.rs#connection-modes)Connection modes

This library provides two way to connect to the [ ControlMaster](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/OpenSSH/Cookbook/Multiplexing):

One is to spawn a new process, the other is to connect to the control socket directly.

The process implementation executes remote commands by invoking the ssh command locally with arguments that make the invocation reuse the connections set up by the control master.

This maximizes compatibility with OpenSSH, but loses out on some fidelity in information about execution since only the exit code and the output of the ssh command is available to inspect.

The native mux implementation on the other hand connects directly to the ssh control master and executes commands and retrieves the exit codes and the output of the remote process over its native protocol.

This gives better access to error information at the cost of introducing more non-OpenSSH code into the call path.

The former parses the stdout/stderr of the ssh control master to retrieve the error for any failed operations, while the later retrieves the error from the control socket directly.

Thus, the error handling in the later is more robust.

Also, the former requires one process to be spawn for every connection while the later only needs to create one socket, so the later has better performance and consumes less resource.

Behind the scenes, the crate uses ssh’s [ ControlMaster](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/OpenSSH/Cookbook/Multiplexing) feature to multiplex the channels for
the different remote commands. Because of this, each remote command is tied to the lifetime of
the

[that spawned them. When the session is](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html)

`Session`[closed](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.close), the connection is severed, and there can be no outstanding remote clients.

[§](https://docs.rs#authentication)Authentication

This library supports only password-less authentication schemes. If running `ssh` to a target
host requires you to provide input on standard input (`STDIN`), then this crate will not work
for you. You should set up keypair-based authentication instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Since we are wrapping the `ssh`, which in turn runs a remote command that we do not control, we
do not have a reliable way to tell the difference between what is a failure of the SSH
connection itself, and what is a program error from the remote host. We do our best with some
heuristics (like `ssh` exiting with status code 255 if a connection error occurs), but the
errors from this crate will almost necessarily be worse than those of a native SSH
implementation. Sorry in advance :)

This also means that you may see strange errors when the remote process is terminated by a
signal (such as through `kill` or `pkill`). When this happens, all the local ssh program sees
is that the remote process disappeared, and so it returns with an error. It does not
communicate that the process exited due to a signal. In cases like this, your call will return
[ Error::Disconnected](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.Disconnected), because the connection to

*that*remote process was disconnected. The ssh connection as a whole is likely still intact.

To check if the connection has truly failed, use [ Session::check](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.check). It will return

`Ok` if the
master connection is still operational, and *may*provide you with more information than you got from the failing command (that is, just

[) if it is not.](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.Disconnected)

`Error::Disconnected`[§](https://docs.rs#remote-shells)Remote Shells

When you invoke a remote command through ssh, the remote command is executed by a shell on the
remote end. That shell *interprets* anything passed to it — it might evalute words starting
with `$` as variables, split arguments by whitespace, and other things a shell is wont to do.
Since that is *usually* not what you expect to happen, `.arg("a b")` should pass a *single*
argument with the value `a b`, `openssh` *escapes* every argument (and the command itself) by
default using [ shell-escape](https://crates.io/crates/shell-escape). This works well in most cases, but might run into issues when
the remote shell (generally the remote user’s login shell) has a different syntax than the
shell

`shell-escape` targets (bash). For example, Windows shells have different escaping syntax
than bash does.If this applies to you, you can use [ raw_arg](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.raw_arg),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html#method.raw_args)

`raw_args`[to bypass the escaping that](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.raw_command)

`raw_command``openssh` normally does for you.[§](https://docs.rs#sftp-subsystem)Sftp subsystem

For sftp and other ssh subsystem, check [ Session::subsystem](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.subsystem) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use openssh::{Session, KnownHosts};
let session = Session::connect_mux("me@ssh.example.com", KnownHosts::Strict).await?;
let ls = session.command("ls").output().await?;
eprintln!("{}", String::from_utf8(ls.stdout).expect("server output was not valid UTF-8"));
let whoami = session.command("whoami").output().await?;
assert_eq!(whoami.stdout, b"me\n");
session.close().await?;
```

[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! the output of the remote process over its native protocol.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! This gives better access to error information at the cost of introducing
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! more non-OpenSSH code into the call path.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! The former parses the stdout/stderr of the ssh control master to retrieve the error
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! for any failed operations, while the later retrieves the error from the control socket
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! directly.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! Thus, the error handling in the later is more robust.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! Also, the former requires one process to be spawn for every connection while the later only
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! needs to create one socket, so the later has better performance and consumes less resource.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! Behind the scenes, the crate uses ssh's [`ControlMaster`] feature to multiplex the channels for
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! the different remote commands. Because of this, each remote command is tied to the lifetime of
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! the [`Session`] that spawned them. When the session is [closed](Session::close), the connection
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! is severed, and there can be no outstanding remote clients.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! # Authentication
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! This library supports only password-less authentication schemes. If running `ssh` to a target
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! host requires you to provide input on standard input (`STDIN`), then this crate will not work
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! for you. You should set up keypair-based authentication instead.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! # Errors
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! Since we are wrapping the `ssh`, which in turn runs a remote command that we do not control, we
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! do not have a reliable way to tell the difference between what is a failure of the SSH
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! connection itself, and what is a program error from the remote host. We do our best with some
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! heuristics (like `ssh` exiting with status code 255 if a connection error occurs), but the
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! errors from this crate will almost necessarily be worse than those of a native SSH
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! implementation. Sorry in advance :)
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! This also means that you may see strange errors when the remote process is terminated by a
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! signal (such as through `kill` or `pkill`). When this happens, all the local ssh program sees
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! is that the remote process disappeared, and so it returns with an error. It does not
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! communicate that the process exited due to a signal. In cases like this, your call will return
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! [`Error::Disconnected`], because the connection to _that_ remote process was disconnected. The
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ssh connection as a whole is likely still intact.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! To check if the connection has truly failed, use [`Session::check`]. It will return `Ok` if the
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! master connection is still operational, and _may_ provide you with more information than you
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! got from the failing command (that is, just [`Error::Disconnected`]) if it is not.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! # Remote Shells
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! When you invoke a remote command through ssh, the remote command is executed by a shell on the
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! remote end. That shell _interprets_ anything passed to it — it might evalute words starting
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! with `$` as variables, split arguments by whitespace, and other things a shell is wont to do.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! Since that is _usually_ not what you expect to happen, `.arg("a b")` should pass a _single_
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! argument with the value `a b`, `openssh` _escapes_ every argument (and the command itself) by
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! default using [`shell-escape`]. This works well in most cases, but might run into issues when
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! the remote shell (generally the remote user's login shell) has a different syntax than the
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! shell `shell-escape` targets (bash). For example, Windows shells have different escaping syntax
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! than bash does.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! If this applies to you, you can use [`raw_arg`](Command::raw_arg),
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! [`raw_args`](Command::raw_args), and [`raw_command`](Session::raw_command) to bypass the
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! escaping that `openssh` normally does for you.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! # Sftp subsystem
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! For sftp and other ssh subsystem, check [`Session::subsystem`] for more information.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! # Examples
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! ```rust,no_run
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! # #[cfg(feature = "native-mux")]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! # #[tokio::main]
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! # async fn main() -> Result<(), openssh::Error> {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! use openssh::{Session, KnownHosts};
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! let session = Session::connect_mux("me@ssh.example.com", KnownHosts::Strict).await?;
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! let ls = session.command("ls").output().await?;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! eprintln!("{}", String::from_utf8(ls.stdout).expect("server output was not valid UTF-8"));
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! let whoami = session.command("whoami").output().await?;
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! assert_eq!(whoami.stdout, b"me\n");
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! session.close().await?;
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! # Ok(()) }
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! ```
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!   [`ControlMaster`]: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/OpenSSH/Cookbook/Multiplexing
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!   [`sshd_config`]: https://linux.die.net/man/5/sshd_config
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!   [`shell-escape`]: https://crates.io/crates/shell-escape
[143](https://docs.rs#143)

#### pub fn [new_process_mux](https://docs.rs#method.new_process_mux)(tempdir: [TempDir](https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.23.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tempfile/dir/struct.TempDir.html)) -> Self

**crate feature**only.

`process-mux`The method for creating a [ Session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html) and externally control the creation of TempDir.

By using the built-in [ SessionBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionBuilder.html) in openssh, or a custom SessionBuilder,
create a TempDir.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use openssh::{Session, Stdio, SessionBuilder};
use openssh_sftp_client::Sftp;
let builder = SessionBuilder::default();
let (builder, destination) = builder.resolve("ssh://jon@ssh.thesquareplanet.com:222");
let tempdir = builder.launch_master(destination).await?;
let session = Session::new_process_mux(tempdir);
let mut child = session
    .subsystem("sftp")
    .stdin(Stdio::piped())
    .stdout(Stdio::piped())
    .spawn()
    .await?;
Sftp::new(
    child.stdin().take().unwrap(),
    child.stdout().take().unwrap(),
    Default::default(),
)
.await?
.close()
.await?;
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/session.rs.html#192-197)

**crate feature**only.

`process-mux`Connect to the host at the given `host` over SSH using process impl, which will
spawn a new ssh process for each `Child` created.

The format of `destination` is the same as the `destination` argument to `ssh`. It may be
specified as either `[user@]hostname` or a URI of the form `ssh://[user@]hostname[:port]`.

If connecting requires interactive authentication based on `STDIN` (such as reading a
password), the connection will fail. Consider setting up keypair-based authentication
instead.

For more options, see [ SessionBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionBuilder.html).

The format of `destination` is the same as the `destination` argument to `ssh`. It may be

password), the connection will fail. Consider setting up keypair-based authentication
instead.

**non-Windows**only.

Get the SSH connection’s control socket path.

Constructs a new [ OwningCommand](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html) for launching the program at path

`program` on the remote
host.Before it is passed to the remote host, `program` is escaped so that special characters
aren’t evaluated by the remote shell. If you do not want this behavior, use
[ raw_command](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.raw_command).

The returned `OwningCommand` is a builder, with the following default configuration:

- No arguments to the program
- Empty stdin and discard stdout/stderr for `spawn`or`status`, but create output pipes for`output`

Builder methods are provided to change these defaults and otherwise configure the process.

If `program` is not an absolute path, the `PATH` will be searched in an OS-defined way on
the host.

host.Unlike [ command](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.command), this method does not shell-escape

unforeseen ways by the remote shell.The returned `OwningCommand` is a builder, with the following default configuration:

- No arguments to the program
- Empty stdin and dsicard stdout/stderr for `spawn`or`status`, but create output pipes for`output`

Builder methods are provided to change these defaults and otherwise configure the process.

[§](https://docs.rs#sftp-subsystem)Sftp subsystem

To use the sftp subsystem, you’ll want to use [ openssh-sftp-client](https://crates.io/crates/openssh-sftp-client),
then use the following code to construct a sftp instance:

```
use openssh::{Session, KnownHosts, Stdio};
use openssh_sftp_client::Sftp;
let session = Session::connect_mux("me@ssh.example.com", KnownHosts::Strict).await?;
let mut child = session
    .subsystem("sftp")
    .stdin(Stdio::piped())
    .stdout(Stdio::piped())
    .spawn()
    .await?;
Sftp::new(
    child.stdin().take().unwrap(),
    child.stdout().take().unwrap(),
    Default::default(),
)
.await?
.close()
.await?;
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/session.rs.html#460-464)

#### pub fn [shell](https://docs.rs#method.shell)<S: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>(&self, command: S) -> [OwningCommand](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html)<&Self>

Constructs a new [ OwningCommand](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html) that runs the provided shell command on the remote host.

The provided command is passed as a single, escaped argument to `sh -c`, and from that
point forward the behavior is up to `sh`. Since this executes a shell command, keep in mind
that you are subject to the shell’s rules around argument parsing, such as whitespace
splitting, variable expansion, and other funkyness. I *highly* recommend you read
[this article](https://mywiki.wooledge.org/Arguments) if you observe strange things.

While the returned `OwningCommand` is a builder, like for [ command](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.command), you should not add
additional arguments to it, since the arguments are already passed within the shell
command.

[§](https://docs.rs#non-standard-remote-shells)Non-standard Remote Shells

It is worth noting that there are really *two* shells at work here: the one that sshd
launches for the session, and that launches are command; and the instance of `sh` that we
launch *in* that session. This method tries hard to ensure that the provided `command` is
passed exactly as-is to `sh`, but this is complicated by the presence of the “outer” shell.
That outer shell may itself perform argument splitting, variable expansion, and the like,
which might produce unintuitive results. For example, the outer shell may try to expand a
variable that is only defined in the inner shell, and simply produce an empty string in the
variable’s place by the time it gets to `sh`.

To counter this, this method assumes that the remote shell (the one launched by `sshd`) is
[POSIX compliant](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/xrat/V4_xcu_chap02.html). This is more or less equivalent to “supports `bash` syntax” if you don’t
look too closely. It uses [ shell-escape](https://crates.io/crates/shell-escape) to escape

`command` before sending it to the
remote shell, with the expectation that the remote shell will only end up undoing that one
“level” of escaping, thus producing the original `command` as an argument to `sh`. This
works *most of the time*.

With sufficiently complex or weird commands, the escaping of `shell-escape` may not fully
match the “un-escaping” of the remote shell. This will manifest as escape characters
appearing in the `sh` command that you did not intend to be there. If this happens, try
changing the remote shell if you can, or fall back to [ command](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.command)
and do the escaping manually instead.

# OwningCommand in openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openssh/0.11.6/openssh/struct.OwningCommand.html

`pub struct OwningCommand<S> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A remote process builder, providing fine-grained control over how a new remote process should be spawned.

A default configuration can be generated using [ Session::command(program)](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.command)
or

[, where](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.arc_command)

`Session::arc_command(program)``program` gives a path to
the program to be executed. Additional builder methods allow the configuration to be changed
(for example, by adding arguments) prior to spawning. The interface is almost identical to
that of [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html)

`std::process::Command``OwningCommand` can be reused to spawn multiple remote processes. The builder methods change
the command without needing to immediately spawn the process. Similarly, you can call builder
methods after spawning a process and then spawn a new process with the modified settings.

[§](https://docs.rs#environment-variables-and-current-working-directory)Environment variables and current working directory.

You’ll notice that unlike its `std` counterpart, `OwningCommand` does not have any methods for
setting environment variables or the current working directory for the remote command. This is
because the SSH protocol does not support this (at least not in its standard configuration).
For more details on this, see the `ENVIRONMENT` section of [ ssh(1)](https://linux.die.net/man/1/ssh). To work around this,
give

[a try. If the remote shell supports it, you can also prefix your command with](https://linux.die.net/man/1/env)

`env(1)``["cd", "dir", "&&"]` to run the rest of the command in some directory `dir`.[§](https://docs.rs#exit-status)Exit status

The `ssh` command generally forwards the exit status of the remote process. The exception is if
a protocol-level error occured, in which case it will return with exit status 255. Since the
remote process *could* also return with exit status 255, we have no reliable way to distinguish
between remote errors and errors from `ssh`, but this library *assumes* that 255 means the
error came from `ssh`, and acts accordingly.

# Child in openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openssh/0.11.6/openssh/struct.Child.html

`pub struct Child<S> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Representation of a running or exited remote child process.

This structure is used to represent and manage remote child
processes. A remote child process is created via the
[ OwningCommand](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html) struct through

[or one of its variants, which configures the spawning process and can itself be constructed using a builder-style interface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.command)

`Session::command`Calling [ wait](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html#method.wait) (or other functions that wrap around it) will make the
parent process wait until the child has actually exited before continuing.

Unlike [ std::process::Child](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Child.html),

`Child` *does*implement

[, and will terminate the local](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop``ssh` process corresponding to the remote process when it goes out of scope. Note that
this does *not*terminate the remote process. If you want to do that, you will need to kill it yourself by executing a remote command like

`pkill` to kill it on the remote side.As a result, `Child` cannot expose `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` as fields for
split-borrows like [ std::process::Child](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Child.html) does. Instead, it exposes

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html#method.stdin)

`stdin`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html#method.stdout)

`stdout`[as methods. Callers can call](https://docs.rs/struct.Child.html#method.stderr)

`stderr``.take()` to get the same
effect as a split borrow and use multiple streams concurrently. Note that for the streams to be
available,`Stdio::piped()` should be passed to the corresponding method on
[.](https://docs.rs/struct.OwningCommand.html)

`OwningCommand`NOTE that once `Child` is dropped, any data written to `stdin` will not be sent to the
remote process and `stdout` and `stderr` will yield EOF immediately.

```
let stdin = child.stdin().take().unwrap();
let stdout = child.stdout().take().unwrap();
tokio::io::copy(&mut stdout, &mut stdin).await;
```

    Remote([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)),
    Disconnected,
    RemoteProcessTerminated,
    Cleanup([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)),
    ChildIo([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)),
    CommandHasEnv,
    CommandHasCwd,
}## Expand description

Errors that occur when interacting with a remote process.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Master)

### Master([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

The master connection failed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Connect)

### Connect([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

Failed to establish initial connection to the remote host.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Ssh)

### Ssh([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

**crate feature**only.

`process-mux`Failed to run the `ssh` command locally.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SshMux)

### SshMux([Error](https://docs.rs/openssh-mux-client-error/0.1.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/openssh_mux_client_error/enum.Error.html))

**crate feature**only.

`native-mux`Failed to connect to the ssh multiplex server.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidCommand)

### InvalidCommand

**crate feature**only.

`native-mux`Invalid command that contains null byte.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Remote)

### Remote([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

The remote process failed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Disconnected)

### Disconnected

The connection to the remote host was severed.

Note that for the process impl, this is a best-effort error, and it *may* instead
signify that the remote process exited with an error code of 255.

You should call [ Session::check](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html#method.check) to verify if you get
this error back.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RemoteProcessTerminated)

### RemoteProcessTerminated

Remote process is terminated.

It is likely to be that the process is terminated by signal.

**NOTE that due to a fundamental design flaw in ssh multiplex protocol,
there is no way to tell  RemoteProcessTerminated from Disconnect.**

If you really need to identify `Disconnect`, you can call `session.check()`
after `wait()` returns `RemoteProcessTerminated`, however the ssh multiplex master
could exit right after `wait()`, meaning the remote process actually is terminated
instead of `Disconnect`ed.

It is thus recommended to create your own workaround for your particular use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Cleanup)

### Cleanup([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

Failed to remove temporary dir where ssh socket and output is stored.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ChildIo)

### ChildIo([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html))

IO Error when creating/reading/writing from ChildStdin, ChildStdout, ChildStderr.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CommandHasEnv)

### CommandHasEnv

The command has some env variables that it expects to carry over ssh. However, OverSsh does not support passing env variables over ssh.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CommandHasCwd)

### CommandHasCwd

The command expects to be in a specific working directory in remote. However, OverSsh does not support setting a working directory for commands to be executed over ssh.

Specify one or multiple jump hosts.

Connect to the target host by first making a ssh connection to the jump host described by destination and then establishing a TCP forwarding to the ultimate destination from there.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/builder.rs.html#300-303)**crate feature **`process-mux` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/builder.rs.html#300-303)

**crate feature**only.

`process-mux`Connect to the host at the given `host` over SSH using process impl, which will
spawn a new ssh process for each `Child` created.

The format of `destination` is the same as the `destination` argument to `ssh`. It may be
specified as either `[user@]hostname` or a URI of the form `ssh://[user@]hostname[:port]`.
A username or port that is specified in the connection string overrides the one set in the
builder (but does not change the builder).

If connecting requires interactive authentication based on `STDIN` (such as reading a
password), the connection will fail. Consider setting up keypair-based authentication
instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/builder.rs.html#320-323)**crate feature **`native-mux` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/builder.rs.html#320-323)

**crate feature**only.

`native-mux`Connect to the host at the given `host` over SSH using native mux, which will
create a new local socket connection for each `Child` created.

See the crate-level documentation for more details on the difference between native and process-based mux.

The format of `destination` is the same as the `destination` argument to `ssh`. It may be
specified as either `[user@]hostname` or a URI of the form `ssh://[user@]hostname[:port]`.
A username or port that is specified in the connection string overrides the one set in the
builder (but does not change the builder).

If connecting requires interactive authentication based on `STDIN` (such as reading a
password), the connection will fail. Consider setting up keypair-based authentication
instead.

[ SessionBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionBuilder.html) support for

`destination` parsing.
The format of `destination` is the same as the `destination` argument to `ssh`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use openssh::SessionBuilder;
let b = SessionBuilder::default();
let (b, d) = b.resolve("ssh://test-user@127.0.0.1:2222");
assert_eq!(b.get_port().as_deref(), Some("2222"));
assert_eq!(b.get_user().as_deref(), Some("test-user"));
assert_eq!(d, "127.0.0.1");
```

# Stdio in openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openssh/0.11.6/openssh/struct.Stdio.html

`pub struct Stdio(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Describes what to do with a standard I/O stream for a remote child process when passed to the stdin, stdout, and stderr methods of Command.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

A new pipe should be arranged to connect the parent and remote child processes.

This stream will be ignored. This is the equivalent of attaching the stream to /dev/null.

The child inherits from the corresponding parent descriptor.

NOTE that the stdio fd must be in blocking mode, otherwise
ssh might not flush all output since it considers
(`EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK`) as an error

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/stdio.rs.html#63-65)#### pub unsafe fn [from_raw_fd_owned](https://docs.rs#method.from_raw_fd_owned)(fd: [RawFd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/os/fd/raw/type.RawFd.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/openssh/stdio.rs.html#63-65)

#### pub unsafe fn [from_raw_fd_owned](https://docs.rs#method.from_raw_fd_owned)(fd: [RawFd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/os/fd/raw/type.RawFd.html)) -> Self

`Stdio::from_raw_fd_owned` takes ownership of the fd passed in
and closes the fd on drop.

NOTE that the fd will be put into blocking mode, then it will be
closed when `Stdio` is dropped.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- `fd`- must be a valid fd and must give its ownership to- `Stdio`.

# KnownHosts in openssh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openssh/0.11.6/openssh/enum.KnownHosts.html

```
pub enum KnownHosts {
    Strict,
    Add,
    Accept,
}
```
## Expand description

Specifies how the host’s key fingerprint should be handled.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Strict)

### Strict

The host’s fingerprint must match what is in the known hosts file.

If the host is not in the known hosts file, the connection is rejected.

This corresponds to `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Add)

### Add

Strict, but if the host is not already in the known hosts file, it will be added.

This corresponds to `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Accept)

### Accept

Accept whatever key the server provides and add it to the known hosts file.

This corresponds to `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no`.
